blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Misra's 1983 paper as a foundational work on distributed termination detection, noting its importance in process networks where detecting when all processes are idle (and no messages are in transit) is crucial. The algorithm uses a marker that traverses processes, painting them white or black to track activity. Colyer emphasizes the elegance of the solution, which can handle arbitrary network topologies, including rings and strongly connected graphs, and even provides a distributed version without global knowledge. The marker-based approach is compared to the Chandy-Lamport snapshot algorithm but predates it. The key insight is using a marker to 'flush out' messages and infer termination by tracking process states over time.
paper_title: Detecting Termination of Distributed Computations Using Markers

Our only assumption is that a process receives (only and all) messages from another process in the order sent by the sender. Our solution is symmetric among the processes, i.e. process id's are not used in the solution. As an application of the scheme in this paper, we give a simple and efficient algorithm for detecting token loss and regenerating the token in a token ring network. The marker algorithm has also been applied [14] in avoiding deadlocks in distributed simulations. A problem of considerable importance in designing computations by process networks, is detection of termination. We propose a very simple algorithm for termination detection in an arbitrary network using a single marker We show an application of this scheme in solving the problem of token loss detection and token regeneration in a token ring.
